cues.text: Let's turn now to responsible design throughout the lifecycle.
The central idea here is that ethics is not something you add at the end of a project, like a coat of paint.
Responsible design means building ethical care into every stage of a system's life, from the first conversation about what to build, right through to the day the data is finally retired.
Let us walk through the six stages in order.
The first stage is requirements.
At this point, the team should identify stakeholders, meaning everyone who is affected by the system, not only the paying customer.
They should identify those stakeholders' needs, and the accessibility requirements, so that people with different abilities can use the system.
They should also ask about data necessity, which means asking whether each piece of data is truly needed.
And they should consider safety and abuse cases, that is, how the system could cause harm, or be deliberately misused by someone.
The second stage is design.
Here, the team should minimise collection, meaning gather as little data as is needed.
They should model threats, which means thinking systematically about how an attacker or a failure could damage the system.
They should choose appropriate authentication and authorisation.
Authentication is proving who you are, and authorisation is deciding what you are allowed to do once you are identified.
They should also establish meaningful consent, so that people genuinely understand what they agree to, and appeal routes, so that a person who is harmed or wrongly refused can challenge the outcome.
The third stage is implementation.

This involves secure coding, dependency checks, which means checking the external libraries and components your software relies on, code review by other people, tests, and documented decisions, so that anyone later can see what was chosen and why.
The fourth stage is testing.

The team should evaluate reliability, subgroup fairness, accessibility, usability, privacy and security, and also realistic failure conditions, meaning what happens when things go wrong in the real world rather than in a perfect laboratory.
The fifth stage is deployment.

This calls for controlled rollout, rather than releasing to everyone at once, along with communication to users, monitoring, and rollback, which is the ability to return to the previous safe version if something goes wrong.
The sixth stage is maintenance.
The team should patch vulnerabilities, reassess data use, handle complaints, audit changes, and retire data responsibly when it is no longer needed.
So, to summarise the sequence: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance.
Each has its own ethical duties.
Now let us look closely at one part of testing, namely fairness.
A fairness test should measure subgroup outcomes rather than only average accuracy.
Here is why.
Suppose we have 100 users in group A, and they experience 95 successful identity checks.
Now suppose 100 users in group B experience only 70 successful identity checks.
The success rates are therefore 95 percent for group A and 70 percent for group B.
These differ by 25 percentage points.
Yet if you simply combine the two groups, the overall success rate is 82.5 percent, which sounds reasonably good.
That overall figure obscures disparate performance, meaning it hides the fact that the system works much worse for one group than for the other.
When you find a gap like this, you should investigate several things: data quality, the model itself, the operating environment, and the decision thresholds.
You should also provide a human review or fallback, so that a person who is wrongly rejected by the automated check has another way through.
Two further points matter.
First, fairness metrics are context dependent and may conflict.
In other words, there is no single measure that is right for every situation, and improving one measure can sometimes worsen another.
Second, context determines how serious an error is.
The harm of denial of healthcare is much greater than a minor recommendation error.
So a system that wrongly denies someone healthcare demands far more care than one that merely suggests a less relevant item.
Finally, let us consider accessible design.

The source gives these examples: screen-reader-compatible labels and focus order, adequate contrast, keyboard navigation, captions, clear language, local-language options, voice alternatives, and responsive low-bandwidth interfaces.
Taking them in turn, labels and focus order let a screen reader announce elements sensibly and move through them in a logical sequence.
Contrast helps people with limited vision.
Keyboard navigation helps those who cannot use a mouse.
Captions help people who cannot hear audio.
Clear language and local-language options help people understand.
Voice alternatives help those who cannot easily type or read.
And responsive, low-bandwidth interfaces help people with weak or expensive internet connections.
One last design consideration concerns offline use.
Offline capture may help continuity, meaning work can carry on when there is no connection.
But sensitive data must be encrypted and synchronised safely.
And there is an important rule for financial transactions: they must never be represented as completed offline without authoritative confirmation.
If a person sees "payment complete" while offline, but the bank has not actually confirmed it, they may be seriously misled.
Only an authoritative confirmation can make that claim true.
